“America, they will tell you, belongs only to those with the right accent or the right shade of skin. The rest of us, they insist, should be grateful for merely being allowed to visit. How small they are. How weak, how unoriginal,” the mayor said.
“The irony” of American exceptionalism, he said, was that the country’s history was often written “by those who were told by others with power and influence and wealth that they were anything but exceptional.”
Mamdani’s office told NBC News this week that the mayor would deliver a “major address” marking the country’s semiquincentennial, another major step onto the national political stage after three of his endorsed House candidates defeated incumbents and incumbent-endorsed candidates in Democratic primaries last month.
Mamdani and Sherrill commemorate 250th anniversary along Hudson River
Ahead of the Sail4th 250 Parade of Sail, featuring 48 tall ships from 20 nations traveling up the Hudson River, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill reflected on the nation's 250th anniversary and the enduring symbol of the New York Harbor.
"Today marks 250 years of our nation and 250 years of millions of people across the world looking upon the greatness that is America," Mamdani said. "That legacy is one that reminds us that the promise of these shores still holds, a promise of opportunity, a promise of freedom, and a promise of self-determination."
Sherrill echoed that message, telling the crowd: "This is America at its best. This is who we are as a people. This is what we can deliver when we fight alongside friends and allies for those things we believe in, and so here's hoping that as we move forward over the next 250 years that we can continue our fight for freedom, for liberty and prosperity."
The parade is one of the marquee events of the nation's celebration of America at 250.
Coast-to-coast festivities mark July 4 and America's 250th birthday
Across the country, Americans are marking Independence Day with celebrations that double as the kickoff to the nation’s yearlong 250th anniversary commemoration.
In Philadelphia, organizers will bury a time capsule to remain sealed until 2276. New York Harbor will host an international Parade of Sail featuring dozens of tall ships and more than 100 military aircraft in an aerial review. Boston will hold its annual parade and the Boston Pops Fireworks Spectacular, while St. Louis welcomes Miranda Lambert for a concert beneath the Gateway Arch and Los Angeles hosts an America 250 concert led by Queen Latifah and Chaka Khan. Chicago’s Navy Pier is capping off the day with its largest and longest Independence Day fireworks display ever.
In Washington, President Donald Trump is set to headline the “Salute to America 250” celebration on the National Mall, followed by a fireworks display and a projection show illuminating the Washington Monument. Meanwhile, in nearby Annapolis, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore is delivering an Independence Day address offering a Democratic counterpoint to Trump's celebration.
Trump marks Fourth of July weekend with speech at Mount Rushmore
President Donald Trump kicked off the nation’s Independence Day weekend yesterday with a speech at Mount Rushmore that blended patriotic celebration with sharp political messaging ahead of America’s 250th anniversary.
Speaking beneath the monument’s four presidential faces, Trump praised the country’s history while warning that a “communist menace” threatens American values, casting communism as a fundamental enemy of the Constitution and the nation’s founding ideals. The address concluded with a fireworks display over the memorial after storms earlier in the evening cleared.
The event also revived discussion about Trump’s place in history, including past efforts by supporters to add his likeness to Mount Rushmore — an idea that geologists and park officials have long said isn’t feasible because the mountain lacks suitable rock for another sculpture.

sources.news_title: Trump mixes patriotism with partisanship in 250th anniversary speech
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump mixed partisan politics with patriotic appeals on Saturday as he commemorated the 250th anniversary of American independence, a moment he declared "one of the most joyous and glorious milestones of all time."
Speaking in Washington after storms prompted a roughly two-hour evacuation of the National Mall, Trump honored veterans, including several from World War II and one of the first Black officers to lead a Special Forces team in combat in Vietnam. They appeared before flags that symbolized some of the most significant and challenging moments in American history, from the one that was draped over Abraham Lincoln's casket to the one that flew on the plane piloted by the Wright Brothers.
Yet Trump also leaned into partisan territory unusual for an Independence Day address, which presidents typically use as a moment to unify the country. Instead, he stumped again for the SAVE America Act, an elections bill that's encountering challenges even from Trump's fellow Republicans in Congress. He highlighted his support for the Second Amendment and revived denunciations of communism, which are becoming an increasingly central part of Trump's message ahead of the November midterms.
The speech capped a holiday that Trump has gone to great lengths to shape to his own tastes. He was introduced by two musical performers who often appear at his trademark rallies, including Lee Greenwood, who performed "God Bless America." The event organizers were largely aligned with the White House, supplanting a bipartisan organization that was launched by Congress a decade ago.
"We will always be on top," Trump said. "We will never let our country fall. We will always be the best."
Trump didn't talk about himself as much as he does during his normal rally speeches. Still, he still found time to include a joke about seeking a third presidential term and about World War II's "greatest generation."
"They are the greatest generation," Trump said. "I hate to admit that, but they are."

sources.news_title: Foul weather forces National Mall evacuation ahead of Trump’s speech
National Mall evacuated due to weather before Trump's speech: USA 250 updates
sources.text:
Trump marks America's 250th with speech and colossal fireworks show
President Donald Trump spoke of historic achievements for the country's 250th birthday, ranging from Revolutionary War victories, to the Lewis and Clark expedition across the West to the success in World War II and the exploration of space.
He was occasionally interrupted by chants of "USA, USA." After Trump finished speaking, a fireworks display of 860,000 pyrotechnics billed as the largest in history got underway just before midnight.
Trump's speech and what he has described as a record-breaking fireworks show got underway hours after severe thunderstorms wreaked havoc on Fourth of July celebrations in the Eastern United States.
From Washington, DC, to Boston, Independence Day events are back on after brief delays due to inclement weather as the country marks its 250th anniversary. Trump’s “Salute to America” event was postponed until 11 p.m. due to “approaching severe weather.” In New York, organizers opted to launch fireworks early to beat weather concerns.
Festivities in Western and Central states, meanwhile, are chugging along as planned, with star-studded concert lineups taking the stage in Nashville and Los Angeles.
"Storms bring luck to whatever the occasion," Trump said in a Truth Social post prior to his speech. "They also make events a little bit more exciting! We will wait it out, I don’t care if it’s 2:00 O’Clock in the morning, or in one hour from now. Looks like it is going to pass, they always do. I will be there no matter what, but the “what” usually turns out to be a good thing."
Earlier, festivities had been hampered by a record-setting heat wave with triple-digit temperatures in parts of the country, including with heat advisories and warnings. The Independence Day parade in the Washington, DC, was canceled due to heat. Parades, fireworks shows and other events were axed or delayed in several states on Friday and Saturday. Still, plenty of people have been braving the weather and uncertainty, turning out for celebrations in major sweltering cities.
Fireworks cap evening of performances at LA Coliseum
Paris Barraza
The thunderous sound of fireworks drowned the roar of the thousands of people marking America's 250th birthday at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum on Saturday.
At one point, "Don't Stop Believin'" by Journey played.
The firework display capped an evening of performances that ended with Chris Stapleton, whose "Tennessee Whiskey" might have united the audience more than any other moment during the America's Block Party Benefit Show — the crowd of thousands sang the lyrics loudly and clearly.
Fog greets fireworks at Golden Gate Bridge
Noe Padilla
Thousands of people lined San Francisco’s shore to witness history, as the city was set to host a fireworks show off the famous Golden Gate Bridge.
Unfortunately, the city’s infamous foggy skies had other plans, as a thick cloud of fog sat over the bridge throughout the day and into the night.
Instead of a captivating burst of fireworks, the Golden Gate Bridge glowed with hues of greens, yellows, reds and more as the fog shielded the display.
However, the show was still a memorable night for many, as the fog provided a unique ethereal image of the bridge.
Regardless, many people leaving Crissy Field could also be heard saying that the show may have been “overhyped.”
Expectations met for 'the greatest fireworks show in history'
Christopher Cann
Greg Buckless, 43, said it was well worth the wait to see tonight’s massive fireworks show in Washington, DC, honoring the nation's 250th birthday.
“I came here expecting the greatest fireworks show in history and I got it,” he said.
The tech worker from New Hampshire was among the thousands who had evacuated the National Mall earlier Saturday because of rain.
Buckless took shelter in the U.S. Department of Commerce Building for several hours before returning for Trump’s speech and the light show.
“I would do this again,” he said. “It’s incredible.”
As the show ended, people quickly filed out of the National Mall. The fireworks had ended and it began to rain again.
Boston revelry ends in 'Happy Fourth'
Bailey Allen
After the fireworks ended there was a mass exodus of guests leaving the Esplanade and flooding the streets of downtown Boston. People walked on the blocked-off Storrow Drive to get to Beacon Street in the city's Back Bay neighborhood.
Thousands streamed out of the area, many loading onto MBTA subway and trolley cars. The pops of unsanctioned fireworks from around the city could be heard in the distance.
Despite the on-and-off rain and the muggy weather, the mood in the city was jovial. Shouts of "Happy Fourth" were heard between revelers, and some people ran through the streets.
Smashing Pumpkins take the stage in LA
Paris Barraza
The Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum may be celebrating America's 250th birthday, but it's also a celebration of live music — as evident by the reaction to the Smashing Pumpkins' set, which included "1979" and "Cherub Rock."
A portion of the crowd was swift to chant for another song after the group’s final performance of the night, as others gathered to their feet to show the band their appreciation.
It's also a celebration of Los Angeles, if evident by an emcee doing a roll call of which cities in the county are represented in the crowd, from Long Beach to Altadena, Santa Monica and Inglewood. Naturally, the roll call played during "California Love."
Crowd cheers huge fireworks display in DC
Christopher Cann
Soon after President Trump wrapped up his speech, a fighter jet flew over the National Mall and what has been billed as the biggest fireworks show in history began.The crowd looked up as the pyrotechnic display colored the sky in shades of red, white and blue.
Cheers broke out at some of the largest bursts of light. Even some of National Guard troops and federal agents could be seen recording the light show on their phones.Most of the crowd packed near the Washington Monument, upon which the words “FREEDOM 250” were displayed.
A band in stage performed “YMCA,” “Livin’ on a Prayer” and “Don’t Stop Believin.’”
Trump honors Artemis II astronauts
Bart Jansen
President Trump honored astronauts from Artemis II who flew around the moon and pledged to send more missions to the lunar surface and to Mars.
The astronauts were joined by Jack Schmitt, the last man to walk on the moon, from the Apollo 17 mission in 1972.
“They flew further from earth than anyone has ever flown before,” Trump said of the Artemis II crew of Victor Glover, Christina Hammock Koch, Reid Wiseman and Jeremy Hansen.
Trump talks vanquishing fascism, and now communism
Josh Meyer
After honoring decorated soldiers from America's wars, President Donald Trump hinted at the current surge of democratic socialist victories in recent U.S. elections − and said communism needs to be stopped.
"They saved the world, and they made America very, very proud," Trump said of the veterans from the Marines, Navy and other U.S. services, noting that, "We vanquished fascism."
Now, Trump said, "America will never be a communist country. Communism is a loser, and it always will be."
"Our warriors did not fight communism on battlefields across the world only to have that menace rear its ugly head right back here in America," Trump said. "We're not going to let it happen, we would like to stop a threat like that immediately, and before it begins."
'We can come together' for this anniversary
Christopher Cann
Sarah Jane, 36, of Virginia, said she didn’t tell some of her friends that she was going to the “Salute to America” event in Washington DC.
She didn’t intend to see President Donald Trump speak, but wanted to see the historic fireworks show.
For the last several years, she spent Independence Day on the National Mall. But since this year’s events were so closely tied to Trump, some of her friends shunned it.
“I don’t agree with most people here but that’s OK,” Jane said. “It’s good to be around people that are different.”
She compared the country’s 250th anniversary celebrations to a relative’s birthday.
“We’re like a dysfunctional family,” she said of her fellow Americans. “But we can come together today for something like this.”
Trump suggests he's serving his third term, not second
Josh Meyer
President Donald Trump, in listing some of his accomplishments while in office, hinted that he's actually serving his third term, in a reference to his oft-stated claims that he actually won the 2020 election that he lost to Democrat Joe Biden.
"We rebuilt our military in my first term. We use it a little in our — actually I should say third term, but I won't do that, because I don't want any controversy," Trump said to some laughter and applause from the audience.
"And we've had tremendous success," Trump said. "You look at Venezuela, you look at Iran; we wiped it out."
Weather disruption makes DC Fourth of July events 'awful' for some
Christopher Cann
Cindy Klempel said the weather had turned the Independence Day celebrations in Washington, DC, into an “awful” affair.
She was among the first in line for the Trump-backed “Salute to America” event on the National Mall.
But after several hours in the sun, her 10-year-old grandniece was falling ill. Klempel brought her to a nearby Smithsonian museum, where she drank water and rested in the air conditioning.
When they went back out, ready to see the fireworks, they learned the event had been delayed because of rain and they would need to wait in another long line.
“This hasn’t been a good day for us,” said Klempel, who traveled to DC from Colorado.
Trump honors flags with original 13 stars
Bart Jansen
President Trump unveiled some of the earliest U.S. flags with 13 stars for the original states, in honor of the July Fourth celebration.
One flag displayed on the stage was from 1777, having flown in the decisive battle at Saratoga, New York. Another was from 1781 in the battle of Yorktown, Virginia, where the British surrendered to end the Revolutionary War.
“These are the real deal,” Trump said.
He later displayed other special flags, including one that covered President Abraham Lincoln's casket, a flag presented to Theodore Roosevelt when he returned from Cuba and one from the USS Arizona that sank in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, at the start of World War II.
“It’s a symbol of American defiance,” Trump said.
Trump says weather delays make this July 4 'an evening for the ages'
Josh Meyer
President Trump says the rain, lightning and bad weather have made the Freedom 250 event in Washington on July 4 "an evening for the ages."
Trump referred almost right away to the bad weather that delayed his speech by more than an hour and forced the evacuation of people from the National Mall.
"In signing their names to the roster of freedom, those 56 patriots put everything at risk, stepped onto the stage of destiny, and seized a victory for the ages, and this is an evening for the ages," Trump said about the signers of the Declaration of Independence 250 years ago.
"I believe this is something very special. This is bigger than if we didn't have the lightning blaring," Trump said. "But this is bigger. Little more inconvenient, but it's bigger, I think in its own way, it's more beautiful."
Trump says 150,000 'special people' in crowd
Bart Jansen
Trump told the crowd he wouldn't let the rain stop him from speaking on the 250th anniversary Independence Day, if it meant talking to one person at 4 a.m.
He said the crowd estimated at 375,000 before an evacuation for lightning storms and 150,000 came back for the speech.
“You’re very special people and we have a very special country," Trump said.
Trump takes stage for July 4th speech
Bart Jansen
Trump took the stage on the National Mall for his speech celebrating the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence.
He was expected to focus on themes of freedom and American grit, as he has in other speeches this week in North and South Dakota.
“I’m not going to let some rain stop our 250th,” Trump said on social media as he left the White House.
Macy’s 4th of July fireworks dazzles NYC skyline as fire breaks out on Brooklyn Bridge
Eduardo Cuevas
Fireworks on New York City’s East and Hudson rivers dazzled the metropolitan skyline as a fire briefly broke out on the Brooklyn Bridge.
The 50th annual Macy’s 4th of July Fireworks show started earlier than scheduled amid severe thunderstorm watch warnings by the National Weather Service.
The viewing of the show took place from the Brooklyn Bridge, but fireworks could be seen across the city. During the show, viewers said they saw a fire break out atop the Brooklyn Bridge. Video showed flames and smoke from the historic 19th-century bridge between Brooklyn and Manhattan.
In an email, the New York City Fire Department said the agency received a call at 9:40 p.m. with a reported “rubbish fire” on the bridge. Firefighters used two engines to extinguish the fire, FDNY said, adding fires such as this aren’t unexpected and that’s why the agency maintains standoff distance during a fireworks show. New York City police referred questions to FDNY.
Outside of official events, the police department earlier warned residents that fireworks are illegal.
“Every year, illegal fireworks cause fires, serious injuries, and even death,” an NYPD social media post said. “As you celebrate July 4th, leave the fireworks to the professionals.”
Cabinet officials join Trump for speech
Bart Jansen
Cabinet officials joined President Donald Trump for the speech, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick could be seen speaking with Trump.
Visitors still in line hope they won't miss Trump's speech: 'He'll wait for all of us'
Christopher Cann
Under a steady drizzle of rain, thousands of revelers stood in line, waiting to get back into President Donald Trump’s “Salute to America” celebration in Washington.
The event was delayed because of thunderstorms and some who had waited hours in line found themselves waiting again. First in extreme heat, then in rain.
Scott Rigsby, a retired sheet metal worker from Atlanta, waited about two hours earlier in the day and never made it inside.
“Well, I’m here,” he said with a chuckle. Rigsby said he hopes Trump doesn’t start speaking before he makes it inside.
“I think he’ll wait for all of us,” he said, as speakers blared “Bohemian Rhapsody.”
Trump arrives with family at National Mall
Bart Jansen
Trump left the White House at 10:03 p.m. and arrived at the National Mall for his speech at 10:09 p.m., according to reporters traveling with him.
Trump could be seen monitoring video coverage of spectators filing back into the mall through metal detectors, after they evacuated briefly under the threat of severe storms.
He got into his limousine surrounded by relatives, including his wife Melania, his sons Don Jr. and Eric Trump, and daughter Tiffany Trump and her husband.
"I’M HERE!!!" Trump said on social media at 10:16 p.m.
Secret Service chief says agents 'doing a great job' getting people through security in DC
Josh Meyer
Secret Service Director Sean Curran is on-scene at the National Mall in Washington and says his agents are "doing a great job" moving the throngs of evacuated people back through security checkpoints so they can hear a speech from President Donald Trump and watch the fireworks show.
"They're keeping up with the flow, and they're doing what they do best," Curran told NBC News' Vaughn Hillyard in a video that showed a large crowd moving briskly behind them.
Trump is scheduled to speak at 11 p.m., followed by what organizers say will be the biggest fireworks display in U.S. history.
America's Block Party gets underway in Los Angeles
Paris Barraza
The performances at America’s Block Party Benefit Show at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum are underway, with Grammy winner Chaka Khan performing under a sun that’s beginning to set on a milestone Fourth of July.
Earlier, country-pop artist Maren Morris sang a short set, and “Hamilton” and “Twisters” star Anthony Ramos performed the national anthem to the thousands of people who gathered at the venue — a crowd filled with folks decked out in red, white and blue.
For hours leading up to the performances, eventgoers stood in line for food and drinks (including bacon-wrapped hotdogs, bags of kettle corn and lemonade) and to pose for photos against an America 250 backdrop.
For Veronica Villa — who had her photo taken — the Fourth of July means being thankful to live in California specifically.
“There are so many opportunities,” said Villa, who is from Pasadena. “There is so much diversity.”
Rain, confetti and fireworks fill the air in Boston
Bailey Allen
Drops of rain began to fall sporadically in Boston as the fireworks began to erupt over the Charles River shortly after 10:15 p.m. Crowds stood still, looking up at the explosive display. The Boston Pops played tunes including "Shipping Up to Boston" by the Dropkick Murphys.
'We weren’t missing this': Excitement as celebrations resume in Boston
Bailey Allen
Sandra Johnson-Jacobs, 70, of Gilbert, Arizona, sat in a beach chair on the grass at the Esplanade in Boston after the rain had stopped falling and the sun had set.
She said she had planned her trip to Boston a year ahead of time, so there was “no way” she was leaving due to a passing storm. She was sitting next to some of her family members from Vermont.
“I wanted someplace special for the 250th and I wanted to get my family together, so, the evacuation added a little excitement to it,” Johnson-Jacobs said. “I felt the water running over my shoes, but I just said, ‘Oh, that’s okay.’ And then I got to come back and watch all this fabulous stuff.”
She was sitting with her son Ryan Johnson, 38, of Milton, Vermont, and 12-year-old grandson Ewan Eichelberger, among other relatives.
Johnson said the family was prepared to stay outside for the remainder of the evening.
“We weren’t missing this. You’re not gonna be around for the next 250th so you might as well tough it out. And we came prepared anyway to go through the storm, got all of our bags and stuff,” Johnson said.
Eichelberger, despite the rain evacuation, was in good spirits.
“Today was just absolutely stunning. I loved it. When the rain was coming, we had to all go in this tunnel, but since the tunnel was filled up with people, we had to stand outside,” Eichelberger said. “I was in my flip flops, and water was just pouring all over my feet. And I was just like, ‘Yep, this is Boston.’”
Long lines as visitors wait to be rescreened at National Mall
Christopher Cann
Lines have formed around 10 p.m. as festival goers wait to reenter tonight's "Salute to America 250" event on the National Mall.
Secret Service officials said everyone will need to be rescreened prior to reentering the event after the threat of storms sent visitors scrambling earlier Saturday.
President Trump is scheduled to deliver his speech around 11 p.m.
Watch the Macy's fireworks light up the New York sky
Long waits won't stop Navy veteran from seeing Trump, fireworks show
Christopher Cann
A long wait isn’t going to stop Kathy Mandakunis and her family from seeing President Donald Trump and a massive July 4 fireworks show.
“Where are we going? We’ve got no place to be,” Mandakunis, 54, said as she, her husband and their two kids sat on a set of stairs in the basement of the Ronald Reagan Building in Washington, D.C., waiting for news about the delayed celebration.
The family had traveled from Salem, Massachusetts, for the event. Much of their day had been spent standing in line, but the military flyovers “broke up the monotony,” said Mandakunis, a Navy veteran.
“Those were so well orchestrated,” she said. “We had a good time, even if it was a little hot.”
Nashville's Fourth of July celebration brings out the stars
Audrey Gibbs
Nashville is living true to its name as the country's "Music City" with Fourth of July celebrations spanning generations and genres.
The "Freedom Sing! Music City July 4th" celebrations in downtown Nashville come with a star-studded musical lineup on multiple stages.
Beginning in the afternoon and continuing at night, The All-American Rejects, Boyz II Men, Brothers Osborne, Clint Black, Lauren Daigle, NE-YO, Nick Jonas and Sublime are all set to perform. The performances are being broadcast live as a Disney TV special, culminating with what city officials said is the largest fireworks and drone show in Nashville's history.
Follow the downtown Nashville events at The Tennesseean, part of the USA TODAY Network.
Secret Service says everyone will go through screening again at National Mall
Josh Meyer
Secret Service spokesman Anthony Guglielmi says the Secret Service screening area "will reopen shortly."
"Everyone who evacuated the site will go through screening again. The Secret Service is working to make screening as smooth as possible," Guglielmi said in an X post at 9:30 p.m. "Our bag restriction and prohibited items list remains the same. For programming information, continue to monitor@Freedom250."
Thousands return to Mall after Trump says speech, fireworks will take place
Christopher Cann
After President Donald Trump said he would speak and the fireworks show would go on, government buildings and museums where people had sheltered began to empty.
Thousands began to queue up outside the event area near the Washington Monument, though the rain hasn’t completely let up yet.
National Mall to reopen, Trump to speak at 11 p.m.
Karissa Waddick
The National Mall will reopen at 9:45 p.m. and Salute to America programming will resume, Freedom 250 Spokesperson Danielle Alvarez said in a statement.
"The President will deliver remarks at 11:00 PM, and the fireworks spectacular will follow. Rain or shine, the American people deserve a celebration worthy of our nation's historic 250th birthday," Alvarez said. "A little rain will never diminish our pride, our patriotism, or our celebration of the greatest nation in the history of the world."
Mass. governor kicks off Boston Pops: 'I'm so proud of our state'
Actor and comedian Jane Lynch took the stage at the Hatch Shell, kicking off the Boston Pops’ performance at the muddy Esplanade.
She introduced Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, who expressed her love of the state – one of the original 13 colonies.
“I'm so proud of our state, from our oceans and Cape Cod, to our mountains across the state, to the Berkshires. This is a state where people do a lot and have done a lot,” Healey said. “They create stuff, they make stuff. We invented the computer, we invented the telephone, first cancer treatments. We invented things like universal access to healthcare and marriage equality. We invented the chocolate chip cookie and fried clams. You can’t beat that.”
Other onstage guests included Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, and musical artists Chance the Rapper, Trombone Shorty and Lainey Wilson.
Many attendees sat on wet grass, while others stayed standing for the remainder of the show. Food trucks reopened after the storm and long lines snaked around the vendor area. Ice cream seemed to be the favorite of the night.
'I’m not standing in line again,' NY woman says before leaving DC events
Christopher Cann
After more than an hour sheltering from the rain, Nadine Szewczyk, 67, decided to head back to her hotel rather than wait for President Donald Trump’s speech and the fireworks show.
“I’m exhausted,” said Szewczyk, who traveled to Washington, D.C., from Albany, New York.
Her day had not gone as planned, thanks to two forms of extreme weather.
It was the morning and afternoon’s extreme heat that forced organizers to cancel the Independence Day parade. Szewczyk had just found the “perfect” vantage point to watch the celebration when someone told her it had been called off.
Hours later, after standing in a seemingly endless line for Trump’s 250 extravaganza, which is set to be capped off by a record-setting fireworks show, the event was delayed because of severe thunderstorms.
She walked to the Ronald Reagan Building, a few blocks from where the event was being held. But after an hour or so, she decided it was time to go.
“I’m not standing in line again,” she said.
Weather, thunderstorm concerns at Philadelphia celebration
Kaitlyn McCormick
Mere hours away from the fireworks show scheduled in Philadelphia, and with people still standing in long lines to enter the festival, a voice could be heard echoing through the Parkway area instructing visitors to head to their nearest entrance, exit or to their vehicles due to weather concerns.
At about 8:44 p.m., the Philadelphia Office of Emergency Management issued a Severe Thunderstorm Warning, set to last through 9:30 p.m.
It is unclear how this may impact the remainder of the concert and the following fireworks display.
It’s a party at the L.A. Memorial Coliseum this Fourth of July
Paris Barraza
Eventgoers at America’s Block Party Benefit Show at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum are snapping photos with a President Abraham Lincoln on stilts, playing corn hole – known as bags to some – and carrying cans of beer.
Among those celebrating the historic moment is Geovanni Agramonte and his wife, Nancy. The husband and wife duo from Lakewood in Southern California just celebrated their 41st anniversary.
It’s the “freedom of everything” that he’s particularly thankful for living in the United States, Geovanni Agramonte said. He is from Cuba.
“I still have a lot of family there,” he said. “They’re suffering right now. So, just the freedom that we have here to just live our lives and try to be a good person and succeed. … I think that’s what I like about it, it’s just the freedom that you have to live your dreams.”
Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness – the Agramontes take it seriously, Nancy Agramonte said.
“I would like to just see people come together a lot more than what it is,” said Agramonte when asked about what he’d like to see of the country moving forward. “We’re pretty divided right now. So, just to see everybody communicate – from a political standpoint, from a nation standpoint – just really come together.”
DC organizers give updated list of shelter areas; one, at the IRS, is already at capacity
Josh Meyer
Freedom 250, the organizer of the July 4th event in Washington, D.C., has updated the list of shelter areas for people on the National Mall who are in the secured perimeter area.
Those evacuating should go to the Department of Education, Internal Revenue Service, Voice of America Building, Thomas Jefferson Memorial, National Museum of American History, National Museum of Natural History, and the Ronald Reagan Building, Freedom 250 said in a post on X.
Minutes later, Freedom 250 said the shelter at the IRS building is at capacity and urged people to seek shelter at the other listed locations.
Freedom 250 will share updates on programming and doors reopening, and urges people to "please stay close to our official channels for updates," spokesperson Danielle Alvarez said in an earlier post asking people to evacuate.
"The safety of our guests, performers, and staff is our top priority," Alvarez said in a 7:32 p.m. post. "Due to approaching severe storms, Freedom 250, United States Secret Service, United States Park Police, National Park Service, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, and all public safety partners are asking all guests to evacuate event grounds and seek temporary shelter in a nearby building."
DC attendees seek shelter
Christopher Cann
Soon after the crowd gathered for President Donald Trump’s “Salute to America” celebration was ordered to evacuate, shelters began filling up.
Within a half-hour, event staff and police began asking people to leave the white tents on the event grounds (where they were initially told to go) and to head to more secure buildings.
Soon, the National Museum of African American History and Culture was at capacity.
Authorities then began directing people to the Ronald Reagan Building, a few blocks away. There, a steady stream of people clad in red, white and blue filled the underground food court.
Large lines formed at some of the only eateries still open. Revelers carried trays packed with burgers, fries or burritos to their tables as they awaited news about the event.
Thousands show up to watch Philly's July 4 concert
Kaitlyn McCormick
Thousands have continued to make their way toward the main stage in front of the Philadelphia Museum of Art for the city’s long-awaited July 4 concert event.
Whether strolling through event tents, grabbing a bite – or a cold treat in the heat – from a barrage of food trucks, or planting themselves in the fireworks-viewing-spot, the Ben Franklin Parkway in Philadelphia is filling up to a performance by Philly’s own Jill Scott.
A slight breeze and lowering sun have broken up the day’s beating heat, setting the atmosphere for a beautiful 250th Anniversary concert.
Boston Pops concert underway
Bailey Allen

The Metropolitan Washington Council of Governments is forecasting "code purple" (very unhealthy) air quality for D.C. and Northern Virginia for July 4 and 5.
Since the 1970s, COG has provided air-quality forecasts and issued health advisories to the media and public when the air is unhealthy.
With code purple and code red, which is one step less dangerous than purple, everyone is at risk for harmful health impacts, according to WUSA9, a local TV news station tracking air quality. It says children, the elderly and pregnant women are especially vulnerable, but even people in good health could experience irritation from pollutants.
Federal environmental officials say that in conditions of “unhealthy” air, or code red and above, people should avoid long or intense outdoor activity and consider moving activities indoors, while those outside should reduce heavy exertion and take more breaks, WUSA9 said. In the “very unhealthy” conditions under code purple, "everyone should avoid long or intense outdoor activity and move activities indoors when possible," it said.

King Charles III wrote a letter to U.S. President Donald Trump and Americans on the 250th anniversary of America's founding, reflecting on the "evolution" of the relationship between the United Kingdom and the United States "from overcoming conflict to forging one of the closest and most productive alliances the world has seen."
Charles congratulated the United States on its anniversary.
"Together, we face the challenges of today, and the opportunities of tomorrow," he said. "As we look ahead to the next 250 years, I have no doubt we will continue to defend our shared values."
Iconic July 4 celebrations kick off. Here's what's happening.
Jeanine Santucci
Here are the big events to look forward to celebrating the Fourth of July and the semiquincentennial:
- Salute to America 250 Celebration and Fireworks: President Donald Trump will speak in the nation's capital at 9:45 p.m. ET. Trump promised his speech would be "really long."
- The Great American State Fair in Washington, DC, will be open through the evening as the Salute to America 250 Celebration kicks off. Military flyovers will continue throughout the afternoon. The fair will run through July 10.
- Fireworks shows around the country are still to come this evening, with the main event in DC kicking off at 10:30 p.m. ET over the Potomac River and Lincoln Memorial, billed as the "world's largest fireworks display." See start times for fireworks shows around the country.
- Sail4th 250, an international maritime celebration described as the largest largest maritime and aerial gathering in U.S. history, kicked off with a fleet of tall ships sailing into New York Harbor. They'll be available to view until July 7.
Earlier events and celebrations
- Earlier on July 4, a crowd gathered outside Independence Hall in Philadelphia to watch a time capsule get buried, not to be opened until 2276, 250 years in the future.
- The U.S. Navy's Blue Angels led a flyover over New York City the morning of July 4, also drawing aircraft from allied countries to celebrate the 250th.
- The Nathan's Famous Hot Dog Eating Contest on Coney Island in New York on July 4, where contestants ate several days' worth of calories in just 10 minutes.
- Trump spoke at Mount Rushmore, where military flyovers and a fireworks show dazzled audiences, the night of July 3.
- The Times Square ball dropped eight times from July 3 to 4, once across each time zone spanning the states and territories.
Who tells the full story of George Washington?
Phaedra Trethan
Under a tent just steps away from the President’s House, where George Washington kept nine enslaved people while he was president and Philadelphia was still the nation’s capital, a series of actors read the stories of those enslaved people, each reading concluding with the words, “I am the American story.”
How that story is told, and by whom, continues to be a matter of legal wrangling and debate: The Trump administration has directed the National Park Service to replace the existing panels explaining the brutality of slavery – and Washington’s role as a slaveholder – with its own panels that critics say downplays both the horrors of slavery and how Washington benefited from the practice.
On Thursday, USA TODAY visited the site, finding some of the original panels in place, and handmade signs in blank spots with anti-Trump messages, suggestions on ways people can learn American history from the perspective of marginalized voices and printouts of Philadelphia Inquirer stories about the back-and-forth between the city (which wants to preserve the original panels) and the Trump administration.
On Saturday morning, those handmade signs were gone, some of the tape used to affix them still in place. By Saturday afternoon, as thousands of people waited in hours-long lines to see the Liberty Bell and Independence Hall just steps away, handmade signs were back, as were new printouts from this morning’s Inquirer about the site.
Sheri Utain from South Philadelphia stood next to one of the walls of the President’s House where some original panels were next to handmade signs. She read text from original panels that were taken down by the National Park Service at the behest of the Trump administration, about the Transatlantic slave trade, the horrors of slavery and George and Martha Washington’s slave ownership.
Why this retiree drove 9 hours to DC's Great American State Fair
Michelle Del Rey
When Donna Festinger learned Massachusetts would not provide funding or resources for the President Donald Trump-backed Great American State Fair, she decided to make sure her state was represented anyway.
The 72-year-old retired teacher drove nine hours from western Massachusetts to the nation's capital, bringing 300 miniature maple syrup bottles and children's coloring books to help stock the state's booth. Her efforts turned the exhibit into a showcase of Massachusetts products and culture instead of one of the sparse displays found elsewhere at the fair.
Massachusetts is one of several states, including Connecticut, North Carolina, Illinois, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island and Washington without an official state-run presence at the event, which runs on the National Mall through July 10. In many cases, volunteers, nonprofits and local organizations have stepped in to fill the void. The Peoria Riverfront Museum, for example, is operating Illinois' booth.
Those grassroots efforts have produced both heartwarming stories and controversy. From residents racing to assemble exhibits on short notice to disputes over displays and sponsorships, the booths highlight the lengths volunteers have gone to ensure their states are represented at the celebration of America's 250th anniversary.
Couple travel from LA to DC for July 4: 'Wouldn’t want to be anywhere else'
Mike Stunson
Paul Ramirez and his husband, Richard Quirk, traveled from Los Angeles to attend America 250 festivities in Washington, DC, and wore matching American flag overalls to celebrate the country’s semiquincentennial.
Ramirez, a 2024 Republican National Convention delegate, previously attended both inaugurations of President Donald Trump with his husband and said “it was very important to be here for the Fourth.”
“I just want to thank President Trump for this amazing birthday party and tribute,” Ramirez said. “This is our second one. We were both in grade school for the bicentennial in ‘76. Now we get to celebrate this in 2026. I don’t think I’ll be around for the 300th, but it’s great to be able to celebrate.”
He said he’s most excited for the night’s fireworks, joking that even people in Alaska will be able to see the show, which Trump promised will be the largest fireworks display in history.
“I wouldn’t want to be anywhere else for the Fourth of July,” Quirk added.
JD Vance rejects 'two-dimensional' views on America's birthday
Jeanine Santucci
Speaking at the Sail4th 250 Parade of Tall Ships in New York Harbor on Saturday, Vice President JD Vance spoke of the history of the country's founding, touted its success, but urged Americans to reject views that focus on the country's darker moments.
Vance read the opening of the Declaration of Independence and said that even 250 years later, the words "command a tremendous power over us as Americans," reminding us of who we are. He said the country being formed by a "conviction that we are bound to one another... by a common character, a shared faith and a shared future." He urged Americans to ignore and reject detractors.
"You will hear a couple small but loud voices today speak obsessively, not of our national greatness but of our national imperfections. They will speak of the powerless and the dispossessed ... If they acknowlege there is anything to be proud of our history, they'll say it's the fact that sometimes the powerless have won," Vance said. "They're wrong."
"They'll talk about America's sins with the anger and zeal of a brimstone preacher but without any of the grace or forgiveness that must be present in the Christian faith," he said. "So what I'd ask you to do, my fellow Americans, on our 250th birthday, is to reject the two-dimensional view of your fellow citizens and reject the two-dimensional view of your country."
What America’s 250th means for one New York family
Amethyst Martinez
Sitting on benches on the riverfront at Battery Park, the Laucella family stood for hours in the beating sun, watching the tall ships go by. In 1976, a similar ship parade happened in the city. Both Robert and Linda Laucella had been on a date to see the July 4 event at just 18 years old.
“We wanted our family to experience this with us 50 years later,” Linda Laucella, the mother, said smiling. “New York is the crossroads of the world.”
They were joined by their three children – Alessandra, Justin and Amora, who were all dressed up in American flag gear.
“They’ve told us about this story since we were kids,” Alessandra Laucella said.
Robert Laucella’s grandparents came over to Ellis Island in 1922, doubling the significance for the family.
“America continues to be a place for everybody,” Amora Laucella told USA TODAY, as she looked out at the Statue of Liberty.
Free water bottles will not run out in Washington, DC, volunteer says
Mike Stunson
Volunteers at the Great American State Fair in Washington, DC said they will not run out of free bottled water as attendees battle the 95-plus degree weather.
John Wilson, a U.S. Army veteran from Leesburg, Virginia, was volunteering at one of the water stations and had thousands of bottles ready to pass out.
“They assured us they’re gonna keep it coming,” he told USA TODAY. “If we get low, they’ll bring us more pallets. We won’t be running out.”
Wilson said he is most looking forward to the day’s military flyovers and the night’s fireworks, in which he will be joined by his fiancée and her mother.
“It’s the 250th anniversary of our country. Where else would you want to be but in DC?” Wilson said. “Regardless of your politics, this is our nation’s capital. It’s 250 years, unbelivable. We made it.”
What it means to sew the American flag
Karissa Waddick
Inside a cavernous warehouse in South Boston, Virginia, thin strips of red and white cotton cascade over nearly every surface. The strips are piled high in plastic bins, sprawled over tables and fed underneath bobbing needles. The whirr of dozens of sewing machines working at once fills the stark, concrete room.
Here at this 200,000-square-foot factory, seamstresses work eight and sometimes 12 hours a day weaving together the American flag.
Their company, Annin Flagmakers, bills itself as the oldest and largest manufacturer of the star-spangled banner in the United States. It is one of few companies still making the flag in America.
Since the company's founding in 1847, Annin flags have marked the country’s highest highs and lowest lows. Its flags hung at President Abraham Lincoln’s inauguration and draped his casket. They flew atop Mount Suribachi after the Battle of Iwo Jima and rocketed to the moon aboard Apollo 11.
Read more about what it means for those sewing the American flag.
NYC ball drops 8 times for America's 250th
Jeanine Santucci
The iconic Times Square ball in New York City made a special appearance for eight drops from July 3 to July 4 to celebrate the United States' 250th anniversary.
The drops were the first time in the ball's history not to happen on New Year's Eve, according to event organizers.
It dropped once in each time zone across the states and territories, with the first drop at 9:45 a.m. ET on July 3 for the Chamorro Time Zone that includes Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands, and the last drop was at 6:45 a.m. ET for American Samoa on July 4.
Thousands line up to visit Great American State Fair in DC
Mike Stunson
A line spanned several blocks late Saturday morning as thousands of people waited to enter the Great American State Fair in Washington, DC on the Fourth of July.
Some guests told USA TODAY they got in the line hours earlier in preparation for the fair to open at noon.
The fair had been opening at 10 a.m. in its opening week, but the day’s oppressive heat led Freedom 250 organizers to delay Saturday’s start.
The heat, which had already reached 95 degrees by 11:45 a.m. ET, also led to the cancellation of the National Independence Day Parade earlier in the day.
Fourth of July in DC will feature seven consecutive hours of military flyovers over the National Mall beginning at 1 p.m. ET. The flyovers will include aircraft from all branches of the military, as well as President Donald Trump’s newly renovated Air Force One.
Locals, visitors celebrate Fourth of July in NYC
Amethyst Martinez
In New York City, celebrators had a plethora of events to choose from to mark the United States' 250th anniversary of its independence.
Elver and Vanessa Radke visited New York City from Connecticut to celebrate. The two stood, holding onto a light pole in Battery Park to get a better view of the Tall Ships parade with planes flying overhead.
“We’re here to celebrate the 250 year anniversary and everything that comes with it — freedom and liberty," Elver Radke said.At the Castle Clinton National Monument, attendees swarmed for a flag raising ceremony which will be followed by an annual Independence Day parade.
Lorraine Bell, a member of the Knickerbocker chapter for Daughters of the American Revolution, was decked out in patriotic pins for the occasion. She was keeping cool with an electric neck fan, and carried frozen water in her bag to beat the heat.
It’s “important to be out here demonstrating that the United States is still alive and well,” she told USA TODAY, adding that the country “still a work in progress.”
As wildfires rage, officials brace for firework danger
Trevor Hughes and Karissa Waddick
Wildfire dangers are particularly high this Fourth of July after an unusually dry and hot winter created dangerously flammable conditions in forests and grasslands across the Western United States.
A single errant firework ember could smolder acres of land.
Some states are already preparing. Utah Gov. Spencer Cox on June 25 issued a rare statewide executive order allowing communities to restrict consumer fireworks, although commercial displays are still permitted.
California State Fire Marshal Dan Berlant said firefighters have already responded to more than a dozen firework-sparked fires in June. "It may be a sign of what is to come here this Fourth of July," he said.
What time will fireworks start?
Karissa Waddick
Fireworks will light up the sky from coast to coast this evening. Here's the timing of some of the largest displays:
- Boston: Fireworks over the Esplanade is slated to start at 9:15 p.m. ET.
- Chicago: A 15-minute firework show over Navy Pier will begin at 10 p.m. CT/11 p.m. ET.
- Philadelphia:The city's fireworks display will begin at 11:30 p.m. ET at the end of a six-hour live concert.
- New York City:The Macy’s Fourth of July fireworks show is expected to begin around 9:25 p.m ET. It will last about 30 minutes.
- Washington, DC: Organizers say show over the Potomac River and Lincoln Memorial will begin around 10:30 p.m ET. It will last nearly 40 minutes.
- Los Angeles: Fireworks at America's Block Party at the LA Memorial Coliseum will begin at 9:15 p.m. PT/12:15 a.m. ET.
Need a recipe for July 4? Try these historical dishes.
Karissa Waddick
Ever wonder what the founding fathers ate? This Fourth of July, you can party like its 1776 with historical recipes.
A group of social media influencers say they've learned a lot about American history by retracing the dietary preferences of the country's leaders – from George Washington's favorite hoecakes to William Henry Harrison’s beloved squirrel stew.
If those don't match your vibe, America's Test Kitchen has pulled together potluck recipes from every state. These South Dakota corncob-smoked ribs, Maryland crabcakes and Oregon Blackberry Piefor your afternoon barbeque.
Patriot Front group spotted in DC
Jeanine Santucci
Members of the Patriot Front, a White supremacist group with hundreds of members nationwide, were spotted around the nation's capital on July 4 wearing their signature blue shirts, chinos and white face coverings.
Photos from Reuters and social media users show the group members taking the metro and gathered at the Eastern Market station in DC Saturday morning.
In video on social media shared by WTOP reporter Mitchell Miller, the group can be seen marching to a drum beat outside Union Station carrying flags that included an upside-down American flag and a Confederate flag.
Demonstrators in Philadelphia protest Iran war, Trump immigration policies
Phaedra Trethan
PHILADELPHIA — Hundreds of people gathered to protest the Iran war and some of President Doanald Trump's policies, marching from Washington Square, where a memorial to the Revolutionary War dead and a statue of General George Washington remind visitors that “freedom is a light for which many men have died in darkness," to proceed to the Museum of the American Revolution.
Among the marchers: ICE Out Philly, a group that opposes immigration crackdowns in the city; the American Friends Service Committee (also known as Quakers) and the Philadelphia Tenants Union.
But perhaps the biggest contingent was Veterans Against Fascism, which organizers said brought between 350-500 veterans from across the country to march bearing signs with messages against the war in Iran, National Guard deployments in cities, military spending and what they say are illegal orders being given to today’s service members.
Lindsay Knapp and Maxine Rebeles were among the many veterans at the square on a sweltering morning. Knapp, who served in the Army and Rebeles, a Navy veteran, both said they wanted to set an example for other veterans and military members that their voices matter, and so do their actions.
“We’re trying to mobilize a community of love,” said Knapp, a Chicago native who came from South Carolina. “We want to model what (activism) looks like. ... We know some people are scared, but the oath we took to the Constitution did not expire.”
Rebeles, who lives in Laredo, Texas, said she’s seen the terror sown by immigration enforcement in her hometown and, as a former educator, saw her students and their parents struggle with the fear of separation and deportation.
NYC prepares for another day of heat as Tall Ships parade draws thousands
Amethyst Martinez
Thousands of locals and tourists alike flooded lower Manhattan Saturday morning to catch a glimpse of the Tall Ships parade while military planes flew overtop.
Dressed in red, white and blue, many carried water bottles and wore sunglasses and hats as the brutal heat is expected to continue throughout the day in the city. As of 10:30 a.m., the temperature was 89 degrees, with an expected high of 97 degrees for the day.
800k without power on 4th of July amid heat
Jeanine Santucci
There are more than 800,000 Americans without power the morning of the Fourth of July amid a brutal heat wave that is sending heat indices soaring, following severe storms the previous day, according to USA TODAY's power outage tracker.
More than 300,000 of those outages are in Michigan, where severe thunderstorms left damage in the Detroit area on Friday, reported the Detroit Free Press, part of the USA TODAY Network. Winds of up to 60 mph moved across the state, utility company DTE Energy said. Most customers are expected to see their power restored by Monday, the company said. Temperatures in Detroit on July 4 are expected to be in the 80s with heat indices in the 90s, according to the National Weather Service, noting the temperatures are more manageable than in recent days.
In New Jersey, over 180,000 were also without power the morning of July 4 due to storms. In Morris County, where over 50,000 lost power, utility JCP&L said there would be a "significant" restoration time, reported the USA TODAY Network's NorthJersey.com. The area is expecting to see a high of 93 degrees on July 4 with a feels-like temperature close to 100.
There were also some 66,000 without power in Pennsylvania, the tracker shows.
U.S. Mint circulates coins honoring America's 250th
Karissa Waddick
The United States Mint has released new currency and collectors items in honor of the country's 250th anniversary. Earlier this year, it unveiled new quarters, dimes and nickels reflecting milestones related to the nation's founding in 1776.
It released five new quarter designs commemorating the Mayflower Compact, Revolutionary War, Declaration of Independence, the U.S. Constitution and the Gettysburg Address quarter. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent scrapped previously approved designs for abolition, suffrage and Civil Rights Movement coins after Trump urged institutions to tell an uplifting story of American history – a move that was criticized by historians as an attempt to “whitewash” the nation’s past.
The Mint has also proposed a $1 coin, commemorative gold coin and $250 bill be printed with Trump's face.
Other commemorative coins honoring the nation's anniversary went on sale June 10.
Military veterans find escape this July 4
Karissa Waddick
Some veterans who experience post-traumatic stress related to loud noises are finding relief this year.
Passageways, a nonprofit that helps veterans in Kansas, is hosting a first-of-its-kind 12‑hour party for a small group of veterans at an underground salt mine museum. The event will feature barbecue ribs and brisket, games, giveaways, sleeping bags, and, notably, no fireworks.
It's the first escape many participants have had in years, the organization's founder, Jennifer Garrison said. After registering for the event, one person told her, "I don't think I have to suffer this year.”
"It brings to front of mind all the veterans that got us to where we are and everything they've been through so that we can have the freedoms we have," Garrison said.
We retraced iconic trips that help define our nation
Journeys have always defined the American spirit. From the earliest pioneering expeditions and nighttime escapes from bondage to the modern-day road trip, Americans are a people on the move – restless, ambitious and innovative.
To honor the nation’s 250th anniversary, USA TODAY and USA TODAY Network reporters are retracing some of the country’s most iconic journeys, taking you from the past into the present to explore, celebrate, and remember who we are as a nation.
Pope Leo urges acceptance of immigrants for nation's birthday
Jeanine Santucci
Leo XIV, the first American-born pope, wrote a letter marking the occasion of the 250th anniversary of his home nation's founding, urging Americans to reflect on their responsibilities to one another and to future generations. He highlighted the principles of religious freedom and the dignity of every human life.
"In this spirit, a full understanding of this dignity leads to recognizing the importance of safeguarding human life from its beginning at conception until natural death, and of building a society in which the vulnerable, the suffering and the forgotten are always met with compassion, solidarity and love," Leo wrote.
He also applied that value to immigrants.
"Defending human life also includes welcoming, protecting and assisting immigrants, whose hopes, sacrifices and contribution have formed part of the history of this country from its very beginning," he wrote.
'A gift to our future.' America250 time capsule buried, to be opened in 2276
Phaedra Trethan
PHILADELPHIA — The time capsule has been buried, not to be opened until 2276.
“That sounds weird,” remarked Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker. “Doesn’t that sound weird?”
The crowd gathered just outside Independence Hall chuckled, and it did indeed feel odd to think about people 250 years from now opening the capsule.
But, as several speakers Saturday morning said, the time capsule is just as much a reflection of who we are and what we value today as it is an expression of optimism for the future, that, as Benjamin Franklin was said to have remarked after the signing of the Constitution, “A republic, if you can keep it,” that in 2025 Americans believed firmly that the nation would endure for another 250 years.
As a bald eagle named Indy occasionally screeched at an offending hawk that flew overheard, speakers talked about the time capsule as a message to future generations about Americans’ hopes, values and lives in 2025.
“Unlike any other burial this one is about hope,” Parker said. “It’s about possibility.”
The capsule is “more than a collection of artifacts,” she continued, “it’s a message from one generation to the next about who we were, what we value and what we thought was worth preserving.”
Tom Caramanico, executive director of the Independence Historical Trust, said the placement of the capsule was deliberate, as a new sculpture by artist John Collins would be placed atop the tract: a representation of Franklin’s famous “Join Or Die” cartoon that urged the separate colonies to unite.
Where will Donald Trump be July 4?
Karissa Waddick
Trump is expected to attend the Fourth of July Fireworks in Washington, DC. He is slated to begin speaking around 9:50 p.m. ET after a performance from Lee Greenwood.
A 40-minute firework show will follow Trump's address.
Washington, DC cancels Independence Day parade
Rebecca Morin
The annual Independence Day Parade in the nation’s capital has been canceled by Washington, DC authorities, due to extreme heat.
The parade was scheduled to begin at 10:30 a.m. ET on July 4. The heat index is expected to reach between 110°F and 115°F, and the National Weather Service issued an extreme heat warning for DC.
The decision was made for the safety of participants, spectators and staff, according to an announcement from DC Mayor Muriel Bowser’s office.
What musical artists are performing July 4?
Karissa Waddick
Major musical acts are performing on televised shows across the country this July 4th. Here's a look at some of the stars that will grace your screen.
- New York City:Post Malone, Blake Shelton, Salt-N-Pepa, Noah Kahan, Bebe Rexha, and Shaboozey will perform during Macy's 4th of July Fireworks Spectacular. NBC will broadcast the show starting at 8 p.m. ET.
- Los Angeles: Queen Latifah will host the America250’s Fourth of July benefit concert at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, with performances from Chris Stapleton, Smashing Pumpkins, Chaka Khan and Anthony Ramos.
- Washington, D.C.: Some of the musical acts performing at Freedom 250's "Salute to America" include the National Symphony Orchestra, Leonard Skynard, Big and Rich, and Lee Greenwood.
- Boston: Performers for the Boston Pops Fireworks Spectacular include Lainey Wilson, Chance the Rapper, the Boston Children's Chorus and the Boston Crusaders Drum and Bugle Corps.
- Philadelphia: Christina Aguilera, Meek Mill, The Roots, Will Smith, Kathy Sledge, Seal, Jordan Davis, Jill Scott and State Property will perform at the One Philly Unity Concert for America.
A sneak-peek at record-breaking firework show planned in DC
Karissa Waddick
Organizers are hoping to break the Guinness World Record for the largest-ever firework show with this year's Fourth of July spectacular in Washington, D.C.
They're planning to launch more than 860,000 shells from 10 locations, including eight barges in the Potomac River, several spots in West Potomac Park and along the Reflecting Pool. The show is expected to last nearly 40 minutes, about double the length it normally runs.
The company that designed the show, Pyrotecnico, said it will include innovative fireworks that most Americans have never seen before.
The show is also expected to start much later than normal. It's not slated to begin until 10:30 p.m. or 11 p.m. after Trump finishes his speech.
Freedom 250 vs. America 250
Karissa Waddick
Two organizations say they're leading the country's 250th anniversary celebrations.
Congress created the bipartisan America250 Commission a decade ago to organize local, state, national, and international commemorations. Under the law, the group must report its activities and spending to Congress.
When Trump took office, he created a group called Task Force 250 to help organize Cabinet-level agencies anniversary initiatives. Then, eight months ago, the president created called Freedom 250 to carry out his vision for the milestone anniversary. Housed under the nonprofit National Park Foundation, Freedom 250 lacks the same transparency as America 250.
America250 organized a July 4th benefits show, called “America's Block Party” in Los Angeles featuring A-list artists, a series of Time Square ball drops marking the start of July 4 in every American time zone and the burying of a national time capsule in Philadelphia. It’s also spearheaded initiatives encouraging charitable giving, entrepreneurial ship and civics participation.
Freedom 250 has planned a prayer rally on the National Mall, the Great American State Fair, the July 4th fireworks special in Washington, DC, an IndyCar grand prix in the nation’s capital and an athletic competition for high school students.
America250 time capsule to be buried in Philadelphia
Phaedra Trethan
PHILADELPHIA — Jennifer Condon, executive vice president of America250, said she “never thought I’d become an expert on the science of time capsules.”
But she is now, and on Saturday morning, more than four years’ work was about to culminate in the burial of a time capsule just outside Independence Hall in Philadelphia.
It felt “like a dream,” she said, and the South Jersey native said it felt like a homecoming to be back in the area where she grew up.
The capsule contains items from every U.S. state and territory and the District of Columbia. The items each represent “all Americans today and the values that we hold,” she said.
Tall ships gather in New York Harbor
Karissa Waddick
More than 30 tall ships from across the globe will sail from the Verrazzano Bridge to the George Washington Bridge on the Hudson River beginning at 9:30 a.m. ET. They will be led by the U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Eagle, known as America's Tall Ship.
Vessels from 46 countries are expected to converge in New York City this weekend in what organizers say will be the largest-ever flotilla of international tall ships and military ships.
USA TODAY recently spent four days aboard the Eagle. Come set sail with us.

sources.news_title: Trump to deliver National Mall address before massive Fourth of July firework celebration
sources.text:
Trump speaks to crowd; slamming Communism before massive Fourth of July fireworks
WASHINGTON (TNND) — In President Donald Trump’s late-night address on Saturday, which was delayed due to storms, he thanked US heroes, praised American ideals, argued to pass the SAVE America Act, and once again slammed communism.
“The communist system is the opposite of the American system, and the communist system has never worked. Our warriors did not fight communism on battlefields across the world, only to have that menace rear its ugly head right back here in America,” Trump slammed Communism.
Around 850,000 firework shells from 10 different sites, including the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the Potomac River barges and West Potomac Park – which may have set a new Guinness World Record for the largest firework display in history.
On Truth Social, President Donald Trump, who didn’t host the fireworks but has touted his prominent place in the Washington celebrations, said the display was the “Best fireworks show, EVER!”
The fireworks show was previously estimated to cost $850,000.
President Donald Trump is expected to take center stage in the country's Independence Day celebration on Saturday night, delivering remarks on the National Mall ahead of what organizers are calling one of the largest fireworks displays ever held in Washington, D.C.
"Despite the heat, which isn’t as bad as predicted, the crowds in D.C. are INCREDIBLE! The love of our Country has never been stronger!" Trump wrote on Truth Social ahead of the event.
"The Air Shows are at a level never seen before -- What great pilots, what great equipment!!! See you all later! Speaking at around 10:00 P.M. at The Lincoln Memorial. The Reflecting Pool looks great, despite all it went through with the Vandal Thugs. Will quickly drain and fix the damage done right after this big weekend. Happy Independence Day. Our Country is Stronger than EVER!!!" Trump added.
The appearance follows Trump's address at Mount Rushmore in South Dakota, where he warned that the U.S. faces a renewed threat from Communism. He urged Americans to recommit themselves to the nation's founding principles as the country celebrates its 250th anniversary.
Speaking beneath the monument honoring Presidents George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Abraham Lincoln, and Theodore Roosevelt, Trump described Communism as "a mortal threat to American liberty" and argued that the ideology poses a greater danger than previous wars and 9/11.
"It is the greatest threat to our country, including World War I, World War 2, Pearl Harbor, or even 9/11," Trump said.
"We're not going to let this happen to us. Believe me, we're not letting it happen," he added. "Because Communism is the enemy of free people. Everywhere, everywhere in the world -- (it) never works. It's the enemy of the Constitution. Above all, it's the enemy of July 4th, 1776. It is the enemy indeed."
The White House, meanwhile, has billed this year's Fourth of July festivities as a celebration of America's semiquincentennial. Saturday's events are expected to include patriotic music, military flyovers, and a large fireworks display over the National Mall.
Thousands of spectators are expected to gather in Washington despite forecasts calling for hot and humid weather throughout the holiday weekend.
The president's remarks will likely focus on the nation's history, military strength, and the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence.

sources.news_title: Freedom 250 event on National Mall evacuated due to severe weather
sources.text:
President Donald Trump mixed partisan politics with patriotic appeals on Saturday as he commemorated the 250th anniversary of American independence, a moment he declared “one of the most joyous and glorious milestones of all time.”
Speaking in Washington after storms prompted a roughly two-hour evacuation of the National Mall, Trump honored veterans, including several from World War II and one of the first Black officers to lead a Special Forces team in combat in Vietnam. They appeared before flags that symbolized some of the most significant and challenging moments in American history, from the one that was draped over Abraham Lincoln's casket to the one that flew on the plane piloted by the Wright Brothers.
Yet Trump also leaned into partisan territory unusual for an Independence Day address, which presidents typically use as a moment to unify the country. Instead, he stumped again for the SAVE America Act, an elections bill that's encountering challenges even from Trump's fellow Republicans in Congress. He highlighted his support for the Second Amendment and revived denunciations of communism, which are becoming an increasingly central part of Trump's message ahead of the November midterms.
The speech capped a holiday that Trump has gone to great lengths to shape to his own tastes. He was introduced by two musical performers who often appear at his trademark rallies, including Lee Greenwood, who performed “God Bless America.” The event organizers were largely aligned with the White House, supplanting a bipartisan organization that was launched by Congress a decade ago.
“We will always be on top,” Trump said. "We will never let our country fall. We will always be the best.”

The National Mall is gearing up for a historic Fourth of July.

But be wary of high heat forecast for Washington this weekend, as event schedules are subject to change amid sweltering temperatures.
Here's the schedule for events on the National Mall, which could be impacted by weather.
America 250 schedule at the National Mall
The events on the National Mall are the culmination of months of programming leading up to America's semiquincentennial. Daytime programming is set to include musical performances and military flyovers along the backdrop of the Great American State Fair. The evening schedule will include a performance from the Joint Armed Forces Orchestra and multiple speakers.
Here's the full schedule of events taking place on the National Mall, according to Freedom 250:
- 1 p.m. ET: Guest entry opens
- 1:15 p.m. ET: Military flyover demonstrations begin
- 5:00 p.m. ET: Opening programming begins
- 7:00 p.m. ET - Salute to America program begins
- 9:45 p.m. ET - Remarks by President Donald Trump
- 10:30 p.m. ET - Fireworks show
If you're planning to spend Independence Day in the nation's capital, anticipate road closures, security screenings, crowded Metro stations and limited parking.
The Great American State Fair
Visitors to the mall on Saturday, July 4 can enjoy booths hosted by some U.S. states featuring activities and programs about their respective areas. Take photos with the Alamo or sit inside a spaceship at the Texas booth, visit Las Vegas at the Nevada booth or enter a raffle for a free vacation at California's booth.
The fair features America 250 merch for sale, food options and interactive exhibits to experience amid scheduled programming.
A presidential address
Despite soaring temperatures, President Donald Trump has promised to deliver a lengthy speech on the National Mall on Independence Day. Trump's remarks will follow a "Salute to America" program and precede a fireworks spectacle.
'Largest Fireworks Show in History'
Prepare to lie on a blanket and gaze at an illuminated night summer sky! Quintessential July 4 fireworks are set for a late start, with the show not expected to open by 11 p.m. ET. Officials say 850,000 firework shells will be launched from 10 sites, with the president calling it the largest fireworks show in history.
If you want a prime spot, be wary of waiting in the heat to save your view. Guests won't have the luxury of bringing certain comfort items, either. Freedom 250 says blankets are allowed, but lawn chairs, coolers, drink tumblers and aerosol sunscreen are prohibited. There will be food and drinks available to purchase at the event, along with free water refill stations. Organizers said the venue will also include misting stations to help attendees stay cool.
The show is expected to be 40 minutes long, meaning you may not head home until nearly midnight. If you want to beat the heat and crowds and watch from home, show will be streamed online at Freedom250.org and on Freedom 250's social media pages.
World Cup fan zone
The 2026 FIFA World Cup continues Saturday with a packed roster of matches. While Team USA won't be on the pitch on July 4, fans are expected to gather at the FIFA Fan Zone on the National Mall in Washington to take in the energy together. Here's who's in the Round of 16 and what's next for the USMNT.
Stay safe amid dangerous heat
All are invited to celebrate America's milestone on the National Mall. But attendees should take caution amid dangerous heat forecasts, with a "feels like" temperature around 109 degrees as crowds gather on the Mall for the day's events.
As the day warms up, following local weather authorities for guidance and check Freedom 250 on X for real-time updates on programming.

sources.news_title: Inside Donald Trump’s Weather-Delayed America 250 Speech and His Push for Voter ID Bill
sources.text:
President Donald Trump spoke late on July 4, 2026, on the National Mall to mark the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.
Severe thunderstorms delayed the event by more than an hour, forcing thousands of attendees to seek shelter in nearby federal buildings and Smithsonian museums.
Trump addressed the crowd for roughly 30 minutes, combining references to American history with criticism of political opponents and a direct call for new election legislation.
Trump stood on a stage positioned between the Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial. He described the United States as stronger than at any point in its history.
He referenced the nation’s founding principles, military victories, and recent advances in space exploration. At one point, he was joined by the four NASA astronauts from the Artemis II mission.
Historic flags from the Revolutionary War and the Wright Brothers’ flight flanked the stage.
The speech shifted to policy when Trump urged passage of the SAVE America Act. The bill would require voter ID and proof of citizenship for federal elections and impose new limits on mail-in ballots.
“Together we are also reasserting the truth that American strength and power is not something to be ashamed of,” Trump said. He presented the legislation as essential to protecting election integrity.
Also Read: July 4 Parade Canceled in Washington as Extreme Heat Disrupts America’s 250th Celebration
Historic Symbols and Official Presence
The event featured multiple symbols of U.S. history. Trump recognized veterans from several wars and highlighted the military’s global record. First Lady Melania Trump accompanied him onstage, along with other family members.
Senior administration officials attended, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Small Business Administrator Kelly Loeffler, and House Speaker Mike Johnson.
Organizers evacuated parts of the National Mall as storms approached shortly after 7 p.m. Gates later reopened, and the program continued despite the delay.
Trump acknowledged the disruption at the start of his remarks, stating there was “no way we can be deterred.”
Warnings on Communism and Ideological Threats
Trump used portions of the speech to warn against what he called the “evil of communism.” He argued that threats once fought abroad had returned domestically and compared the issue to a cancer that must be removed quickly.
The comments echoed language from his earlier Mount Rushmore appearance ahead of the anniversary.
Also Read: Jack Smith Warns Trump’s Jan. 6 Pardons Could Threaten Midterm Elections
He avoided extended discussion of current foreign policy crises but focused on domestic divisions.
Trump said Americans who fought communism overseas should not see it reemerge at home. The remarks drew clear partisan lines during an event intended to commemorate national founding.
Election Legislation and Political Context
The push for the SAVE America Act formed a central policy section of the address. Trump tied the bill to maintaining national strength and preventing fraud.
Details of the legislation have circulated in Congress, though its prospects remain tied to Republican majorities in the House and Senate.
The speech occurred against a backdrop of other July 4 developments, including Trump’s recent pardons and separate violence in New York’s Coney Island. Democratic leaders offered differing reactions to the anniversary events, with some criticizing the partisan tone.
The 250th anniversary events continue through the weekend with additional programming in Washington and across the country.
